python_int_lesson_1:slide:0.title: What is OOP? 🏗️
python_int_lesson_1:slide:0.content:
Object-Oriented Programming organizes code into objects - bundles of data and functionality.

Key concepts:
• **Class**: A blueprint for creating objects
• **Object**: An instance of a class
• **Attributes**: Data stored in an object
• **Methods**: Functions that belong to an object

python_int_lesson_1:slide:1.title: Why Use OOP? 💡
python_int_lesson_1:slide:1.content:
Benefits of OOP:

✅ **Modularity** - Code is organized into self-contained units
✅ **Reusability** - Create once, use many times
✅ **Maintainability** - Easy to update and fix
✅ **Real-world modeling** - Objects represent real things

python_int_lesson_1:slide:2.title: Creating a Class
python_int_lesson_1:slide:2.content: Use the class keyword to define a blueprint.

python_int_lesson_1:slide:3.title: The self Parameter 🔑
python_int_lesson_1:slide:3.content:
**self** refers to the current instance of the class.

It allows you to:
• Access attributes: self.name
• Call methods: self.bark()
• Distinguish instance from class variables

python_int_lesson_1:question:0.explanation: __init__ is the constructor that sets up initial state when an object is created.

python_int_lesson_1:question:1.explanation: self refers to the current instance of the class being created or used.

python_int_lesson_1:question:2.prompt: How do you create an object from class Dog?
python_int_lesson_1:question:2.explanation: In Python, you create objects by calling the class name like a function: Dog()

python_int_lesson_1:question:3.explanation: Each lesson objective is to build practical skill with one focused concept.

python_int_lesson_2.title: Inheritance
python_int_lesson_2.description: Learn how to reuse code with class inheritance

python_int_lesson_2:slide:0.title: What is Inheritance? 🌳
python_int_lesson_2:slide:0.content:
Inheritance allows a class to inherit attributes and methods from another class.

Terminology:
• **Parent/Base class**: The class being inherited from
• **Child/Derived class**: The class that inherits
• **Override**: Replace parent method in child

python_int_lesson_2:slide:1.title: Why Inheritance? 🎯
python_int_lesson_2:slide:1.content:
Benefits:

✅ **DRY** - Don't Repeat Yourself
✅ **Hierarchy** - Model real relationships
✅ **Extend** - Add features without changing original
✅ **Polymorphism** - Same interface, different behavior

python_int_lesson_2:slide:2.title: Creating Child Classes
python_int_lesson_2:slide:2.content: Pass the parent class in parentheses.

python_int_lesson_2:slide:3.title: Using super() 🦸
python_int_lesson_2:slide:3.content: super() calls the parent class methods.

python_int_lesson_2:question:0.explanation: super() allows calling methods from the parent class.

python_int_lesson_2:question:1.prompt: How do you create a child class?
python_int_lesson_2:question:1.explanation: In Python, put the parent class name in parentheses: class Child(Parent)

python_int_lesson_2:question:2.explanation: Override means defining a method in child class with same name as parent to replace behavior.

python_int_lesson_3:slide:0.title: List Comprehensions ✨
python_int_lesson_3:slide:0.content:
List comprehensions provide a concise way to create lists.

Syntax: [expression for item in iterable]
With filter: [expression for item in iterable if condition]

python_int_lesson_3:slide:1.title: Why List Comprehensions? 🚀
python_int_lesson_3:slide:1.content:
Benefits:

✅ **Readable** - Clear intent in one line
✅ **Fast** - More efficient than loops
✅ **Pythonic** - The "Python way"
✅ **Flexible** - Filter and transform together

python_int_lesson_3:slide:2.title: Basic Examples
python_int_lesson_3:slide:2.content: Transform and filter data in one line.

python_int_lesson_3:question:1.prompt: What does [x for x in range(5) if x > 2] return?
python_int_lesson_3:question:1.explanation: Only values greater than 2 pass the filter: 3 and 4.

python_int_lesson_3:question:2.prompt: Which is equivalent to: result = []; for x in items: result.append(x*2)?
python_int_lesson_3:question:2.explanation: List comprehension syntax: [expression for item in iterable]

python_int_lesson_4:slide:0.title: Lambda Functions ⚡
python_int_lesson_4:slide:0.content:
Lambda functions are small anonymous functions.

Syntax: lambda args: expression

Perfect for short, one-time functions.

python_int_lesson_4:slide:1.title: Lambda vs Regular Functions 🆚
python_int_lesson_4:slide:1.content:
Comparison:

**Regular function:**
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

**Lambda function:**
add = lambda a, b: a + b

Use lambda for simple, single-use operations.

python_int_lesson_4:slide:3.title: Lambda with map() & filter() 🔧
python_int_lesson_4:slide:3.content: Use lambda with functional programming tools.

python_int_lesson_4:question:0.prompt: Correct lambda to add two numbers?

python_int_lesson_4:question:1.explanation: Lambda functions can only contain a single expression, not multiple statements.

python_int_lesson_4:question:2.prompt: What does map(lambda x: x**2, [1,2,3]) return?
python_int_lesson_4:question:2.explanation: map() applies the lambda to each element: 1²=1, 2²=4, 3²=9

python_int_lesson_5:slide:0.title: Try/Except 🛡️
python_int_lesson_5:slide:0.content:
Handle errors without crashing your program.

Common exceptions:
• ValueError - wrong value type
• TypeError - wrong operation on type
• ZeroDivisionError - divide by zero
• FileNotFoundError - missing file

python_int_lesson_5:slide:1.title: Why Handle Exceptions? 💡
python_int_lesson_5:slide:1.content:
Benefits:

✅ **Graceful failure** - App doesn't crash
✅ **User-friendly** - Show helpful error messages
✅ **Recovery** - Try alternative approaches
✅ **Logging** - Track errors for debugging

python_int_lesson_5:question:0.explanation: finally always executes, regardless of exceptions.

python_int_lesson_5:question:1.prompt: How do you catch ANY exception?
python_int_lesson_5:question:1.explanation: A bare "except:" catches all exceptions (though "except Exception:" is preferred).

python_int_lesson_5:question:2.explanation: raise creates and throws an exception that can be caught by try/except.
